{"id": "28:20/q01", "question": "How did Moses' killing become known and lead to the warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the Egyptian or an unnamed enemy exposed the killing, and whether Pharaoh had learned of the plan before the warning.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q01/p1", "position": "The Egyptian heard the Israelite disclose the earlier killing, told the Copts or Pharaoh's council, and Pharaoh or his chiefs sought Moses' death.", "reasons": "Yahya's Qatada identifies the last Egyptian; Tabari's Ibn Abbas, Abu Bakr's companions and Ibn Abi Najih, Wahidi, Baydawi, Alusi, and Study Quran link the exposure to the Israelite's words in 28:19. Wahidi says he informed the Copts; Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Qurtubi, Ibn Ashur and Kur'an Yolu report Pharaoh's death or arrest order. Ibn Ashur cites Exodus for Pharaoh hearing and seeking Moses' death. Islahi says the secret's spread naturally prompted the plan. Muqatil and Biqai say the slain person was a Copt; Wahidi cites Ibn Abbas and Muqatil that it was yesterday's Egyptian."}, {"id": "28:20/q01/p2", "position": "An enemy overheard Moses' exchange and spread the accusation.", "reasons": "Tabari reports Ibn Jurayj's wording that an enemy heard and broadcast what he heard; it leaves the hearer's identity less specific than the Egyptian reports."}, {"id": "28:20/q01/p3", "position": "The man knew of the chiefs' plan and warned Moses before Pharaoh was informed.", "reasons": "Qushayri's Israelite acquaintance reports the leaders' plot and urges departure before they tell Pharaoh, unlike reports that Pharaoh had already ordered his death."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q02", "question": "Who was the man who warned Moses?", "turns_on": "Reports disagree over family or Israelite affiliation and over the man's name; Ibn Atiyya questions certainty about the names.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q02/p1", "position": "A believer from Pharaoh's family, commonly named Hizqil, described by some as Pharaoh's cousin.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls him the believing Copt Hizqil ibn Sabuth; Thalabi and Qurtubi give Hizqil ibn Sabura, Mawrdi Hizqil ibn Shamaun, Bursevi Khirbil. Reports differ in spelling and patronymic. Zajjaj adds carpenter; Kalbi calls him Pharaoh's paternal cousin; Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, and Qurtubi also call him cousin. Ibn Jurayj in Durr says Hizqil was not a notable. Thalabi, Baghawi, Razi, and Qurtubi ascribe this to most exegetes; Wahidi cites Ibn Abbas and majority. Alusi prefers the well-known family identification; Islahi considers it probable and connects him to Sura al-Mu'min. Ibn Jawzi points to a discussion in Ghafir. Some reports only identify the family believer without a name."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p2", "position": "His name was Shim'un or Shama'un, a name also connected with Pharaoh's family believer.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim and Thalabi transmit Shuayb al-Jubbai; Tabari's Ibn Jurayj transmits Shuayb through Wahb. Mawrdi, Baghawi, Tabarsi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Durr, Itqan, and Alusi report forms of the name. Qurtubi cites Daraqutni that Sham'an with shin is known only as the family believer; Abu Hayyan separately reports Shamaun ibn Ishaq. Ibn Atiyya cautions that firm claims about names are remote."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p3", "position": "His name was Sam'an or Shama'an.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim attribute Sim'an or Sam'an to Ibn Ishaq; Thalabi, Mawrdi and Ibn Atiyya transmit related forms. Baghawi, Tabarsi, Qurtubi, Itqan and Alusi list the alternative. The reports vary in consonantal spelling and vowels; Ibn Atiyya cautions against certainty."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p4", "position": "He was an Israelite or a partisan and acquaintance of Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas calls him Moses' partisan; Qushayri an Israelite acquaintance. Baghawi calls him one of Moses' adherents; Ibn Ashur and Study Quran report an Israelite possibility. Ibn Ashur also says the site of his arrival signals he knew Moses. The affiliation can overlap with some unnamed accounts but differs from identification as Pharaoh's kinsman."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p5", "position": "He was an Egyptian who believed secretly.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur suggests that God may have guided the man's sound nature to recognize the corruption of idolatry and prepared him to save Moses."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p6", "position": "His name was Talut.", "reasons": "Qurtubi attributes this identification to Suhayli."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p7", "position": "His name was Jibril ibn Shamaun.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this name from Kalbi."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p8", "position": "He was another, unspecified person.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports 'someone else' alongside the believer identification; Abu Hayyan and Alusi likewise preserve an alternative identity. Ibn Atiyya finds confident naming remote."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p9", "position": "His name was Sharwan.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi's Nuzha gives this as an alternative to Hizqil."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p10", "position": "His name was Jabr.", "reasons": "Itqan lists it among transmitted names."}, {"id": "28:20/q02/p11", "position": "His name was Habib.", "reasons": "Itqan lists it among transmitted names."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q03", "question": "What moved the man to warn Moses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q03/p1", "position": "He cared for Moses and sincerely wanted to save him.", "reasons": "Biqai calls him one who loves Moses; Razi says concern made him hurry; Ibn Ashur cites admiration for Moses' uprightness; Islahi sees sympathy in a courtier running to Moses' settlement. Alusi links his haste to distance and eagerness to advise. Tabari calls him Moses' partisan. Biqai says the emphatic assurance counters any assumption that the king's favor made danger unlikely."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q04", "question": "What does the city's farthest part denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether the geographical phrase merely describes the outskirts or permits inference about the palace and rulers' quarter.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q04/p1", "position": "The remote edge or outskirts of Pharaoh's city.", "reasons": "Tabari specifies Pharaoh's city; Wahidi and Ibn Jawzi gloss farthest and most distant; Bursevi notes the root's distance sense. Ibn Ashur distinguishes Abu Tammam's line about a settled city center becoming an edge, and cites 33:13 for another usage. Samarrai says this order can describe the man's residence or his point of departure."}, {"id": "28:20/q04/p2", "position": "The remote part was probably Pharaoh's palace or ruling quarter, away from the Israelite settlement.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reasons that rulers lived at city edges for security against revolt or raids and easier escape; the messenger's origin suggests proximity to the court and acquaintance with Moses. Tabatabai infers the palace stood beyond the city and the conspiracy was ordered by Pharaoh. Islahi locates the rulers' center far from the Israelites' quarter."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q05", "question": "How does 'from the farthest part of the city' attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "The phrase's attachment determines whether the wording fixes the man's departure point or characterizes where he belonged; Alusi rejects an attachment to yas'a.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q05/p1", "position": "It modifies 'came,' giving the place from which he arrived.", "reasons": "Alusi calls this the most natural attachment. Tabatabai says it grammatically qualifies 'came.' Abu Hayyan allows it, and Samarrai says it makes the origin definite in the comparable word order. Ibn Ashur's palace inference rests on the man coming from that direction."}, {"id": "28:20/q05/p2", "position": "It describes the man, indicating his origin or residence.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says the phrase has specified the indefinite man; Baydawi, Nasafi, Samin, Alusi, and Samarrai allow the adjectival phrase, with yas'a a further modifier or circumstantial clause. Samarrai says this can denote a resident of the far end, not necessarily a departure from there."}, {"id": "28:20/q05/p3", "position": "It attaches to 'hurrying.'", "reasons": "Alusi mentions this proposed construction but dismisses it as implausible."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q06", "question": "What does 'yas'a' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether sa'y specifies rapid movement, simple walking, work, or a figurative spiritual aim; reports differ on whether the speed was running.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q06/p1", "position": "He hurried on foot, moving rapidly toward Moses.", "reasons": "Yahya's Suddi, Ibn Qutayba, Tabari's Ibn Jurayj, Kalbi, Wahidi's Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jawzi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur gloss haste. Ibn Qutayba says sa'y commonly denotes rapid walking and may include running; Ibn Atiyya prefers hurrying and cites Malik's treatment of going to Friday prayer, while Zajjaj and others there say short of running. Ibn Ashur compares 20:20 and 17:19; Alusi takes the literal haste as apparent because of distance and eagerness. Baghawi describes hurrying on foot along a near route."}, {"id": "28:20/q06/p2", "position": "He ran quickly.", "reasons": "Zajjaj explicitly says running; Ibn Qutayba allows running within sa'y's range. Biqai emphasizes speed that outstripped others, and Muqatil says he ran on foot."}, {"id": "28:20/q06/p3", "position": "He was walking on his feet.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Wahidi transmit Muqatil's basic on-foot gloss; the reports do not specify speed."}, {"id": "28:20/q06/p4", "position": "He was working or exerting himself.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this from Ibn Jurayj as an alternative to haste, despite Tabari's report from Ibn Jurayj giving haste."}, {"id": "28:20/q06/p5", "position": "He sought God's good pleasure.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a figurative interpretation and compares the wording of 17:19."}]}

{"id": "28:20/q08", "question": "How did the warning man reach Moses before the pursuers?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports specify a shortcut and pursuit routes or only the man's urgent arrival.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q08/p1", "position": "He took a short or side route and outran Pharaoh's messengers, who used the main road or searched other byways.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas in Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Thalabi says Pharaoh's executioners took the main road while Moses' partisan took a shortcut. Baghawi says the man arrived first and warned Moses to use another route; Tabarsi, Ibn Kathir and Biqai likewise emphasize the short route and urgency. Suddi in Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim says Pharaoh had Moses sought along side paths, thinking the young man did not know them; Moses nevertheless took them. Ibn Kathir says this explains the man's description as active. Tabari's Qatada says the warning reached Moses at his far-off location."}, {"id": "28:20/q08/p2", "position": "He hurried to warn Moses, without a specified route.", "reasons": "Tabari's Qatada simply places the man at Moses' distant location; Qurtubi says he hurried after Pharaoh ordered execution. Qushayri says the acquaintance hurried before Pharaoh was notified. Kur'an Yolu says a well-wisher ran to advise escape."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q09", "question": "Why is the order of 'a man' and 'from the farthest part' different from 36:20?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q09/p1", "position": "Al-Qasas uses the ordinary or less definite order for a private warning; Ya Sin foregrounds the remote origin for a public mission and surprise.", "reasons": "Burhan says Ya Sin preposes the place to make readers wonder whether everyone rejected the messengers, whereas Qasas retains normal order. Samarrai contrasts Ya Sin's public call against a hostile town (36:18, 36:20) with Moses' private warning and says public proclamation deserves fronting; the two orders also differ in how firmly they state origin or residence. Samin notes these are different men and stories. Biqai links Qasas's subject-first order to the gravity of this moment."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q10", "question": "What does the indefinite 'rajul' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q10/p1", "position": "It introduces one particular man.", "reasons": "Burhan and Itqan explicitly take the indefinite as a single individual. Itqan also surveys other possible functions of indefiniteness elsewhere: a kind or type (21:50, 2:7, 2:96), magnification (2:279, 3:21, 19:15, 37:109, 9:72), abundance or abundance with greatness (26:41, 6:34), and small quantity (9:72, with a poet's line that a little from the beloved suffices). These are general comparisons, not claims that rajul has each of those senses here."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q11", "question": "What is the function of 'he said' and the address 'O Moses'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q11/p1", "position": "Calling Moses by name signals affection and makes the addressee certain.", "reasons": "Biqai connects the direct address with the man's concern for Moses."}, {"id": "28:20/q11/p2", "position": "The speech clause is a substitution of inclusion for the man's arrival.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur parses qal as badal ishtimal because arriving includes speaking."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q12", "question": "Who are 'al-mala' here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q12/p1", "position": "Pharaoh's influential Coptic notables or governing council.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Ibn Jawzi, Bursevi, Alusi, and Study Quran gloss leaders, nobles or a council; Zajjaj notes others look to them. Biqai says they possess authority to decide and command. Ibn Ashur explains their consequence and cites 7:60; Study Quran points to other hostile notables in stories of Sheba, Quraysh, Hud, Shuayb and Joseph's king (27:29, 38:6, 7:65, 7:88, 12:43)."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q13", "question": "What does 'ya'tamiruna bika' mean?", "turns_on": "Lexical force of reciprocal ifta'ala, evidence from poetry and 65:6, whether consultation can be malign, and whether the verb alone denotes mere intent.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q13/p1", "position": "They consult or deliberate with one another about Moses' death.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, Tabari, Kalbi, Zamakhshari, Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, and others use mutual counsel. Tabari cites an anonymous ta'tamir line and al-Namir's yu'tamar; Majaz cites al-Namir and Rabia ibn Jashm, whose line warns that apparently good judgment may ruin one. Mawrdi, Thalabi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Samin, and Jishumi cite poetic parallels, including a poet's line on deliberating over every event; Mawrdi also cites Imru al-Qays. Wahidi's Shammar says consultation may be wise, desire-driven or fallible self-consultation, illustrated by a proverb about confusion. Ibn Atiyya argues ifta'ala can be reciprocal like tafa'ala, citing izdawaja and 65:6. Ibn Ashur derives consultation from accepting another's order, supports it with 65:6, and says an implied intention remains; Baydawi, Biqai, Bursevi and Alusi say each participant commands and complies. Qurtubi's Azhari allows both counsel and reciprocal command. Wahidi endorses Abu Ubayda and Zajjaj as compatible; Ibn Qutayba rejects this sense as contextually ill-suited, though Wahidi disputes him."}, {"id": "28:20/q13/p2", "position": "They intend or resolve evil against Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba argues consultation is ordinarily good and does not fit a murder plot; Ibn Tulub's verse about someone following his own opinion illustrates intent and its potential error. He treats 65:6 as resolving on a good course, so neither spouse harms the other; he says mutual consultation would require yata'amaruna fika. Wahidi reports this reading but denies Arabic uses i'tamara bi-shay' for mere intending. Majaz and Thalabi combine intention with counsel; Ibn Ashur says consultation implies intent."}, {"id": "28:20/q13/p3", "position": "They command or urge one another to kill Moses.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Azhari, and reports in Thalabi, Mawrdi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Tabarsi, Ibn Jawzi, Nasafi and Samin explain reciprocal exhortation. Azhari prefers it to Ibn Qutayba's mere intent; he, Thalabi and Mawrdi cite 65:6 for commanding one another to good, while Abu Hayyan cites 2:233. Wahidi treats command and counsel as compatible. Ibn Atiyya reports Ibn Qutayba as supporting command but rejects his restriction on reciprocal ifta'ala, invoking 65:6 and al-Namir; the reports of Ibn Qutayba's exact gloss diverge."}, {"id": "28:20/q13/p4", "position": "They are watching or lying in wait for Moses.", "reasons": "Jishumi records this as a reported interpretation without argument."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q14", "question": "How does 'bika' work in the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q14/p1", "position": "The pronoun is genitive after the preposition ba'.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives the case explanation."}, {"id": "28:20/q14/p2", "position": "The ba' marks what the council intends to do to Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur connects the preposition with the implied object of their consultation and murderous intention."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q15", "question": "Why do the chiefs mean to kill Moses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q15/p1", "position": "They had heard he killed an Egyptian Copt the previous day and decided to kill him for it.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya's Qatada, Wahidi's Ibn Abbas and Muqatil, Qurtubi, Biqai, and Islahi connect the decision with the revealed killing; Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim report Pharaoh's order and searches. Ibn Ashur says the consultation implies the case reached Pharaoh, matching Exodus. Kur'an Yolu says Pharaoh ordered his capture once the killer was known."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q16", "question": "What is Moses told to leave?", "turns_on": "Literal flight from a threatened city versus Qashani's inward symbolic city.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q16/p1", "position": "He must leave the city or Egypt immediately to escape the chiefs.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Baghawi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Bursevi and Islahi specify the city; Tabarsi specifies Egypt. {"id": "28:20/q18", "question": "What governs the advanced phrase 'laka'?", "turns_on": "Whether relative al in al-nasihin bars its complement from appearing before it, or whether broader adverbial or definite-article analyses allow it.", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q18/p1", "position": "It is an explanatory lām attached to an understood expression of advice, rather than governed by al-nasihin.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Kashshaf, Tabarsi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi and Alusi say a complement cannot precede the relative al or its clause; Nasafi compares 'welcome to you,' Alusi 'sugya laka.' Abu Hayyan and Samin report an omitted 'advisor for you' or an explicative phrase. Tabarsi says it attaches to an understood word. Alusi calls this the majority grammatical view."}, {"id": "28:20/q18/p2", "position": "It can attach to al-nasihin through a permitted advanced complement or broad adverb usage.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this among three grammatical positions; Samin allows broad adverb usage; Alusi reports grammarians who permit advancement before this al or treat al as a definite article."}]}

{"id": "28:20/q21", "question": "What does the verse imply about warning someone of danger?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q21/p1", "position": "Disclosing a plot against someone is permissible when it serves a religious interest.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes this inference to Qurtubi and others; the warning man's action supplies the example."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q22", "question": "How does the story continue after the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q22/p1", "position": "Moses fled on an unfamiliar route and sought God's rescue.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says Moses trusted the man, escaped pursuit alone, and relied on God; Kur'an Yolu says he left for Midian. {"id": "28:20/q23", "question": "What inward reading is given to the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q23/p1", "position": "The visitor is love or will arising after the self's desire is killed; it warns against the faculties' plot and drives Moses toward spirit.", "reasons": "Qashani reads the far city as hidden preparedness, the slain one as desire, and the fast messenger as love. {"id": "28:20/q25", "question": "How does Moses' warning bear on Muhammad and the Meccans?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q25/p1", "position": "Moses' rescue invites Meccans to recognize Muhammad's character and foreshadows his departure and rescue from oppression.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares the appeal to reason about Muhammad's lifetime among his people in 10:16 and sees the warning as a hint of his later exit from Mecca."}]}
{"id": "28:20/q26", "question": "Why does this Moses narrative interrupt and recur with distinct wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q26/p1", "position": "The man's arrival interrupts an omitted exchange because it is more important; repeated Moses episodes each convey their own nuance.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the man arrives during Moses' exchange with the Egyptian and the dialogue is omitted at the interruption. {"id": "28:20/q28", "question": "How does context distinguish the senses of a flexible Arabic interrogative?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q28/p1", "position": "The context selects whether anna asks how, from where, or when.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi's Nuzha reports Ibn Qutayba's paired 'how' and 'from where' senses and possible interchange, al-Kumayt's line combining them, and Ali ibn Ubayd Allah's rule that state, place and time determine the reading. {"id": "28:20/q29", "question": "How does sincere advice here contrast with Satan's claim to advise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:20/q29/p1", "position": "Satan's claimed counsel deceived Adam, whereas true safety calls for seeking refuge in Allah.", "reasons": "Razi says Satan once worshipped God but was expelled for refusing to honor Adam; he then opposed humankind despite people's obedience to him. Razi says seeking refuge in the name Allah invokes the one worthy of worship whose power, knowledge and wisdom jointly deter wrongdoing: power without knowledge may be evaded by a thief, and both without wisdom may tolerate evil. These are a broader thematic comparison to the verse's sincere adviser."}]}
{"id": "28:21/q01", "question": "From where, and in what circumstances, did Moses leave?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:21/q01/p1", "position": "He left Pharaoh's city in Egypt after warning of a plot to seize him.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, Thaʿlabī, Qushayrī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Bayḍāwī, Nāṣafī, and others identify the departure as from the city or Egypt.
